section.title: Bless the LORD, You Servants
section.sectionRationale: The last of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, this closing pilgrim song sends worshipers into the night with a call to bless the LORD and a benediction in return, forming the fitting final word of the whole Ascents collection.
section.thesis: Worship is not bound to daylight or festival crowds; the night watch servants of the LORD are called to bless Him continually, and He answers, blessing His people in return from Zion, the Maker of heaven and earth.
section.frameNote: One short movement in three lines: the call to the night watch servants to bless the LORD (v1), the physical gesture of lifted hands (v2), and the LORD's answering blessing from Zion (v3).

verses.text: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD!
Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and {{barak|bless}} the LORD!
May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.

barak.gloss: To bless, kneel, or praise. The same root describes both the people blessing the LORD in worship and the LORD blessing His people in return, a two way exchange of covenant favor.

basic.context: The final Song of Ascents, sung as pilgrims' festival visit to Jerusalem drew to a close. It turns from the pilgrims themselves to address the temple servants who kept watch through the night, urging them to keep worship going long after the daytime crowds had gone home.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes a specific liturgical exchange between departing worshipers and night watch priests, and by extension calls every generation to see that God's praise is not limited to daylight, festival, or public settings.
basic.originalLanguages: The single Hebrew root barak, to bless, carries the whole psalm: worshipers bless the LORD with lifted hands, and the LORD in turn blesses them from Zion, showing worship as a genuine two way exchange rather than a one directional demand.
basic.typology: The night watch in the earthly temple anticipates the call to unceasing prayer and praise in the church, a sacrifice of praise offered continually, Hebrews 13:15, and looks forward to the new creation where God's presence needs no night at all, Revelation 22:5.
basic.christ: Christ is greater than the temple, Matthew 12:6, and in Him access to God's presence and blessing is no longer confined to the sanctuary or its hours; through Him believers themselves become a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices continually, 1 Peter 2:5, 9.
basic.god: God is presented as the Maker of heaven and earth, fully able to bless from Zion those who bless Him, tying His cosmic power directly to His covenant faithfulness toward His worshiping people.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 6:24-26 gives the priestly blessing this psalm echoes in reverse. Hebrews 13:15 calls believers to a sacrifice of praise offered continually. 1 Peter 2:5 and 9 names believers a holy priesthood. Revelation 22:5 pictures worship needing no night at all.
basic.oneStory: The night watch blessing of the earthly temple anticipates the church's calling to unceasing praise in Christ, and points forward to the new creation, where God's people will serve and bless Him forever in unbroken day.

context.literary:
Three verses, three appearances of the covenant name, and one verb that turns around in the middle of the poem. In verses 1 and 2 the people are told to bless the LORD; in verse 3 the LORD is asked to bless them. The same Hebrew verb, barak, stands at the start and the end, but its subject and object trade places. That reversal is the whole shape of the psalm, a small circle of blessing going up and blessing coming down.

The grammar moves with it. Verses 1 and 2 are plural commands, addressed to a company, and the verse 1 opening is the little word hinneh, which means look or behold, a cry to wake people up. Verse 3 changes to a singular you, so one voice speaks over many, or over each person in turn. The place changes too. The first two verses are set in the house of the LORD, in the night, with hands raised toward the holy place. The last verse reaches out to Zion, and beyond Zion to the Maker of heaven and earth, so a gesture made in a dark courtyard ends up addressed to the one who made the whole sky.

The psalm also closes a journey. The collection opens in Psalm 120 with a voice far from home, saying 'Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar,' Psalm 120:5. It ends here, inside the house, in the small hours, with nothing left to ask for except that God would bless. The title for God in verse 3 is one the pilgrim songs have used twice already, Psalm 121:2 and Psalm 124:8, 'the Maker of heaven and earth,' and in Psalm 134 the help that was promised on the road has become a blessing received at the destination.
context.historical:
The temple never fully slept. Chronicles records that the Levite musicians 'were on duty day and night,' 1 Chronicles 9:33, and that the gatekeepers 'would spend the night stationed around the house of God, because they were responsible for guarding it and opening it every morning,' 1 Chronicles 9:27. Under the law of Moses the lamps in the sanctuary were to be tended 'from evening until morning,' Exodus 27:21, and the incense was kept burning before the LORD, Exodus 30:7-8. Someone was always on shift. Psalm 134 speaks to those people, the ones whose work was done after the crowds had gone to their lodgings.

The first hearers were pilgrims. Israel's men were to appear before the LORD three times a year, Deuteronomy 16:16, and the Songs of Ascents were the travelling songs of those journeys. Psalm 122:1 captures the arrival, 'I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD.' By Psalm 134 the feast is over or nearly so. The pilgrims are about to go back to their towns, and as they pass the courts they hear the watch on duty, or they call out to them. Isaiah 30:29 knows of 'the night of a holy festival' on which Israel sings, which shows that night worship was a recognised part of the feasts, not an invention of this psalm.

The raised hands are an ordinary posture of prayer in Israel. Solomon spread out his hands toward heaven at the dedication, 1 Kings 8:22, and David pictured 'my uplifted hands' as 'the evening offering,' Psalm 141:2, and prayed with his hands lifted 'toward Your holy sanctuary,' Psalm 28:2. Later Jewish tradition connects the fifteen Songs of Ascents with the fifteen steps in the temple on which Levites sang during the festival of Booths. That tradition is late and the psalm does not mention it, but it fits the picture of Levites standing in the night to sing. The psalm has no title naming an author or occasion, so its date is not fixed by the text.
context.canonical:
Psalm 134 and Psalm 135 meet at the seam of the Psalter's Book V. Psalm 134 ends with a blessing 'from Zion.' Psalm 135 ends with 'Blessed be the LORD from Zion, He who dwells in Jerusalem,' Psalm 135:21. Psalm 135:19-20 then calls on the house of Israel, the house of Aaron, the house of Levi and those who fear the LORD to bless, which is a wider echo of the 'servants who stand in the house of the LORD' in 134:1. It is as though the closing blessing of the pilgrim songs is picked up by the whole congregation in the next psalm.

The blessing in verse 3 also leans on older texts. The priests were set apart to 'pronounce blessings in His name,' Deuteronomy 10:8 and Deuteronomy 21:5, and the words they used are given in Numbers 6:24-26, ending with God's promise, 'they shall put My name on the Israelites, and I will bless them,' Numbers 6:27. The pairing of blessing with the Creator goes back to Melchizedek, who blessed Abram by 'God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth,' Genesis 14:19, and to Psalm 115:15, 'May you be blessed by the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' Psalm 133:3 is the immediate neighbour: 'there the LORD has bestowed the blessing of life forevermore.' The place of blessing is Zion in both psalms.

The New Testament carries the psalm forward in several directions. Anna 'worshiped night and day,' Luke 2:37, and Paul and Silas were singing hymns 'about midnight,' Acts 16:25. Jesus' last act on the Mount of Olives was to lift up His hands and bless His disciples, Luke 24:50-51, and they went back to the temple 'praising God continually,' Luke 24:53. The call to lift up hands is repeated for the church in 1 Timothy 2:8, and the unbroken praise of heaven, 'day and night they never stop,' Revelation 4:8, is the fullest form of what the night watch was doing in part.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted the pilgrims to leave the temple knowing something about the people who stayed behind. Those who serve by night are easy to forget. No one sees their work, no one thanks them, and nothing in the daylight liturgy depends on them being noticed. The psalm therefore does two things at once. It tells them that what they do is worship, not only duty, and it gives the departing worshipers words with which to honour them.

It also meant to leave the last word with God. The final verse is a prayer in the jussive, a wish that the LORD would act, rather than a statement about what the worshipers have earned. The psalm sets the gesture of the hands against the greatness of the One addressed, 'Maker of heaven and earth,' so that a small human offering is received by a God who needs nothing and still bends toward a people in a courtyard. The whole pilgrim collection has been a movement toward God's house and toward blessing, and the author intends this short psalm to say, in the plainest words available, that this is what the house is for: to bless and be blessed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a snapshot of one particular liturgy. It does not command the Levites to stand at night or give a rule for how many should serve. Those arrangements come from Chronicles and the law, and they belonged to the temple of that age. The command in verses 1 and 2 is limited to 'servants of the LORD' in the house, and there is no instruction here that every believer must keep vigil.

What the psalm does model, and what other Scriptures commend, is the pattern underneath the practice: that praise does not need an audience, that the hidden hours belong to God, that raised hands are an honest way to say you are asking for nothing but his face, and that blessing comes back down from the One who is blessed. Applied today, this does not mean copying the rota. It means taking seriously those who work when others sleep, and allowing the night, whether it is a literal night shift or a season of darkness, to be a place where the LORD is blessed too.

debates.question: Who are the servants who 'serve by night' in verse 1?

views.label: The priests and Levites on night duty
views.case: Chronicles describes exactly such a watch, 1 Chronicles 9:27 and 9:33, and Exodus 27:21 assigns the lamps to Aaron and his sons from evening until morning. 'Servants' who 'stand' in the house fits those on duty.

views.label: The pilgrims themselves, keeping a night vigil at a feast
views.case: The collection is a pilgrim collection, and Isaiah 30:29 refers to singing 'as on the night of a holy festival.' 'Servants of the LORD' is used elsewhere of all God's people, for example Psalm 135:1, so the psalm may address the whole company.

views.label: Both, with the Levites standing for the whole congregation
views.case: The Levites were set apart to bless and serve on behalf of Israel, Deuteronomy 10:8, so a call to them can work as a call to everyone they represent.

debates.bearing: Whichever group is meant, the verbs are the same, and so is the practical lesson. The people most likely to be overlooked are told that what they do in the dark is worship, and the rest are invited to join them.

debates.question: Does verse 2 mean 'lift up your hands to the sanctuary' or 'lift up your hands in holiness'?

views.label: Toward the holy place
views.case: This is how most English versions render it. It fits Psalm 28:2, 'toward Your holy sanctuary,' and the physical direction of Israelite prayer toward the house of God.

views.label: In holiness, or in the holy place
views.case: The Hebrew word qodesh can mean holiness as well as the holy place, so the verse can be read as a call to worship in a holy manner. 1 Timothy 2:8, 'lifting up holy hands,' resembles this sense.

debates.bearing: The two readings are closer than they look, since the holy place is where holiness meets the worshiper. Neither changes the central point that the posture of the hands answers the greatness of God.

debates.question: Who speaks verse 3, and to whom?

views.label: A priest or Levite answering the departing pilgrims
views.case: The change from plural commands to a singular blessing fits a single priestly voice, and it resembles the pattern of Numbers 6:24-26.

views.label: The pilgrims, blessing the night watch
views.case: The psalm belongs to the pilgrim collection, so travellers may be leaving a parting wish for those who keep the house.

debates.bearing: The ancient reader of the Psalter would hear both. The point of the verse is not the speaker but the direction: the last blessing is asked of the LORD, and it flows from Zion.

study.originalLanguages:
Hinneh, the first word, is usually left out of English or turned into 'come.' It means look, see, and in verse 1 it works like an alarm bell. Whoever is listening is told to pay attention to the thing in front of them, which is that the night watch, who might think no one is listening, are standing in the house of the LORD. The same word is the one that opens Psalm 133:1, so the last two Songs of Ascents both begin by pointing at something worth seeing.

The verb for what the servants do in the house is the ordinary Hebrew verb for standing. Standing is the posture of service in the sanctuary. Deuteronomy 10:8 says the Levites were set apart 'to stand before the LORD to serve Him.' The English 'serve' in the BSB covers a verb that literally says they stand, and the picture is of a person on duty, upright, in front of the One he serves. The reference to night makes the posture more demanding, since standing watch is harder in the dark.

The command in verse 2 is se'u yedekem, 'lift up your hands.' The verb nasa, to lift, is the common one for lifting hands in prayer, and the phrase that follows, qodesh, has the range noted above, holy place or holiness. The plural 'hands' matters too: both hands, an empty and open gesture. The mouth says barak, the hands say nasa, and together they make one act of worship.

Barak itself has an interesting range. Its root is often linked to the word for knee, which suggests kneeling, and the sense moves from an act of respect to speech that praises. When people 'bless' God, as in verses 1 and 2, the verb is directed up, and it cannot add anything to God. When God 'blesses' people, as in verse 3, the same verb is directed down and does what it says: it gives life, favour and increase. The psalm uses one verb for both movements, and the grammar teaches that worship is a relationship, with the two directions never mixed up.

The final verse uses the form yevarekhekha, with the third person jussive and a singular 'you.' It is not a flat statement, 'The LORD blesses you,' but a wish for that blessing, in the same mood as the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24, 'May the LORD bless you and keep you.' The title 'Maker of heaven and earth' is a participle, oseh, 'making' or 'the one who makes,' which presents creating as a defining, continuing character of the LORD, and not only a past event. The verse therefore bases the blessing on who God always is.

The Septuagint numbers this psalm 133 and keeps the same shape. Its verb for blessing is the familiar word from which the church's own language of blessing comes, which helps explain why Christian worship has used this psalm for evening prayer.

typology.type: The night watch of the temple
typology.fulfillment: The Levites who stood watch in the house of the LORD at night were a small group doing, for all Israel, the work of unceasing praise. The New Testament extends that calling to every believer, who is told to 'continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,' Hebrews 13:15, and to 'pray without ceasing,' 1 Thessalonians 5:17. The escalation is that the whole church is now the priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9, so the watch is not delegated. The type falls short because the Levites served in a building and by rota, while the church worships in every place and its unceasing prayer rests on Christ's own priesthood, not on its own endurance.

typology.type: The blessing coming down from Zion
typology.fulfillment: Verse 3 sends blessing out from the sanctuary toward the people. In Christ this becomes concrete: God 'has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms,' Ephesians 1:3, and Jesus' last act on earth was to lift His hands and bless His disciples, Luke 24:50-51. Zion in Hebrews 12:22 is no longer a hill but the heavenly Jerusalem to which believers have already come. The type falls short in that the old blessing was asked for and awaited, while the new is given and sealed in the Spirit, though believers still wait for its full inheritance, Ephesians 1:13-14.

typology.type: The raised hands in the sanctuary
typology.fulfillment: Lifted hands toward the holy place pointed the worshiper to where God had put His name. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming when the Father would be worshiped 'neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem' but 'in spirit and in truth,' John 4:21-24, because the true temple was His body, John 2:19-21. Paul can now ask that the men everywhere pray 'lifting up holy hands,' 1 Timothy 2:8, without any pilgrimage to a particular hill. The type falls short because the gesture itself was never the point; the sanctuary toward which the hands were lifted was a shadow, and in Christ the believer approaches the throne of grace itself, Hebrews 4:16.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ along three lines, all of them about worship and blessing. The first is the sanctuary. The hands are lifted toward the holy place because that is where the LORD had chosen to put His name. Jesus is the one who says that 'something greater than the temple is here,' Matthew 12:6, and John reports that He was speaking about 'the temple of His body,' John 2:21. In Him the dwelling of God among His people stops being a building and becomes a person, 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. The place toward which the night watch lifted their hands has come to the people in the night.

The second is the priesthood. The Levites stood 'to serve Him' and 'to pronounce blessings in His name,' Deuteronomy 10:8, but they were many, and they died. Hebrews presents Jesus as 'a great high priest who has passed through the heavens,' Hebrews 4:14, and invites believers to come to the throne of grace 'with confidence,' Hebrews 4:16. What they once did on behalf of the nation, He does, once and for all, and no one now stands at the door to ask whether the hour is right. Because He has 'released us from our sins by His blood' and 'made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:5-6, the royal priesthood of the church can bless God day and night, 1 Peter 2:9.

The third is the blessing itself. The psalm ends in a wish that blessing would flow from Zion. Jesus fulfils it twice over. In life, He is the one through whom God 'has blessed us ... with every spiritual blessing,' Ephesians 1:3. At His departure, He lifted up His hands and blessed His disciples, and 'while He was blessing them, He left them,' Luke 24:50-51. The picture is of the final priestly blessing, given with raised hands, and it makes the disciples go back to the temple 'praising God continually,' Luke 24:53. They bless God because He has blessed them in the way the psalm hoped.

None of this requires reading the night watch as a code for Christ. The psalm is about real servants in a real temple. But the pattern it traces, God's people blessing God and God blessing them from Zion, is the pattern fulfilled in Jesus, who is both the one who gives the blessing and the one through whom believers offer theirs. The way is open and the watch is shared. Even the night in which He was betrayed, when Judas 'went out into the night,' John 13:30, became the night in which He gave Himself to His own, so that the hours of darkness are no longer a place God's people face without blessing.
study.god:
Psalm 134 puts two names for God side by side in a single sentence. He is 'the LORD,' the covenant name that appears once in each verse, and He is 'the Maker of heaven and earth.' The first name belongs to Israel's history with Him: Zion, His house, His servants, His promise to bless, Numbers 6:27. The second belongs to the whole world. The psalm refuses to separate them. The God who has a particular address in Jerusalem is the same God without whom nothing exists, and the blessing that comes from a particular hill comes with creation's whole authority behind it.

That is a more demanding picture than it first looks. The Maker of heaven and earth cannot be fed by what worshipers bring or improved by what they say, as Solomon admitted at the dedication, 'Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built,' 1 Kings 8:27. Yet the psalm calls for blessing the LORD, and does not treat it as a trivial request. God is not made greater by praise, but He is honoured by it, and He has chosen to be addressed in this way, Psalm 135:1-2. Greatness and nearness are held together without explanation.

The psalm also shows God as the one who is awake. The night is not empty. The LORD who neither slumbers nor sleeps, Psalm 121:4, is the one to whom the watch is offered, and the same Psalm 121:2 has already named Him 'the Maker of heaven and earth' as the source of help. Those who serve by night are not alone with the dark. They keep company with the God who is present in it, and who also did His great work of creation and rescue in the dark, at midnight in Egypt, Exodus 12:29, and in the long hours of the nights of Israel's history.

Finally, the psalm shows God as the giver of the last word. The people bless God, but the psalm does not end with their blessing. It ends with His. This is how the whole book of Psalms treats worship: its summit is not our praise but His response, a grace that reaches us because He is first a God who gives. For worship, this means two things. It means the worshiper should come with open, lifted hands, expecting to receive. And it means that when the service is over, and the lights are low, the people of God leave not with a duty done but with a blessing spoken over them, from Zion, by the One who made everything.

crossReferences.note: The priestly blessing. Psalm 134:3 uses the same verb and the same wish form, 'May the LORD bless you,' and adds the name 'Maker of heaven and earth.' Verse 27 explains why it matters, because the priests put God's name on the people and He Himself promises to bless them.

The neighbouring psalm ends with the LORD commanding the blessing 'there,' on the mountains of Zion. Psalm 134 takes the same place and the same blessing and turns it into the final prayer of the collection, so that one picture of unity flows into one of worship.

The first appearance of the title 'Maker of heaven and earth' in the Songs of Ascents, placed in the mouth of a traveller looking toward the hills. In Psalm 134 the traveller has arrived and the title becomes the ground of blessing rather than of help.

The next psalm repeats the call to bless, now directed to Israel, Aaron, Levi and all who fear the LORD, and ends with 'Blessed be the LORD from Zion.' Together the two psalms make a single hinge, with one psalm leaving the house and the other filling it.

The historical background in a single verse: the Levite musicians stayed in the temple chambers and were 'on duty day and night.' It shows that the night watch of Psalm 134 was an actual rota, and that singing was part of the work, not an extra.

David asks that his prayer be like incense and his uplifted hands like the evening offering. It joins the raised hands of Psalm 134:2 to the sacrificial evening hours and explains why lifted hands in the night counted as worship in their own right.

The risen Jesus lifts His hands and blesses the disciples, and they return to the temple praising God continually. It is the nearest New Testament parallel to the psalm's two directions, blessing given and blessing returned, and it happens on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple.

Paul and Silas, in prison and in pain, sang hymns to God about midnight while the other prisoners listened. It shows the night watch released from the temple walls and taken into the dark places where the church now lives and worships.

Believers are told to offer 'continually' a sacrifice of praise through Jesus. The temple's night shift has become a calling for all God's people, resting not on rota or place but on the priestly work of Christ.

In the new Jerusalem 'His servants will worship Him' and 'there will be no more night.' It is the psalm's own picture completed, with servants still serving, God's name on their foreheads, and no darkness left to keep watch against.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 134 is a very small psalm placed at an important point in the story. The Songs of Ascents begin with a person scattered among strangers and end with people standing in the house of God in the night. That is a compact version of the Bible's own movement: from exile and separation toward the presence of God, from Eden's closed gate to a house where His servants stand before Him. The psalm does not tell the whole of that story, but it stands where the road arrives.

Behind the psalm lie the first blessings of Genesis. God blessed the creatures and the man and the woman at creation, Genesis 1:28, and promised Abram that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. Verse 3 of the psalm draws on both. It names the God who made heaven and earth and asks for the blessing He attached to Abraham's family to come down on a particular company of servants, so that the pilgrims go home as carriers of the promise. The priestly blessing of Numbers 6 is the means, and Zion is the place.

Ahead of the psalm stand Jesus and the church. Jesus is the offspring through whom the nations are blessed, Genesis 22:18, and His final gesture was a blessing from raised hands, Luke 24:50. The church receives that blessing and answers with praise that does not stop. Peter speaks of a people who 'proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light,' 1 Peter 2:9. Night, in this vocabulary, is both literal and spiritual, a symbol for the darkness out of which they were called and a place in which they keep watch.

The story ends in the new creation, where the psalm's wish is fully answered. 'No longer will there be any curse,' and God's servants 'will worship Him,' with 'His name on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:3-4. There is 'no more night in the city,' Revelation 22:5, and the gates 'will never be shut at the end of the day,' Revelation 21:25. The watch can be stood down. The Maker of heaven and earth will have made the new heaven and the new earth, and the blessing from Zion will be the permanent condition of those who live there, praising Him in a day that does not end.

quiz.q: Who does Psalm 134 specifically call to bless the LORD?

options.text: The servants of the LORD who serve by night in His house.
options.note: Verse 1 names exactly this group, the temple's night watch.

options.text: Foreign kings and their armies.
options.note: The psalm addresses temple servants, not foreign rulers.

options.text: Only the high priest alone.
options.note: The call is plural, to 'all you servants,' not to one individual priest.

options.text: Farmers bringing their harvest offerings.
options.note: The psalm's setting is the temple's night watch, not agricultural offerings.

quiz.q: What physical gesture does verse 2 call for in worship?

options.text: Lifting up hands to the sanctuary.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly commands, 'Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD.'

options.text: Bowing the face to the ground in silence.
options.note: Other psalms describe bowing, but this verse specifically names lifted hands.

options.text: Removing sandals as at holy ground.
options.note: This gesture belongs to Moses at the burning bush, not to this psalm.

options.text: Clapping in rhythm with musical instruments.
options.note: The psalm names lifted hands, not clapping.

quiz.q: How does verse 3 describe the LORD who blesses His people?

options.text: The Maker of heaven and earth.
options.note: This exact title appears in verse 3, tying cosmic power to covenant blessing.

options.text: The God of Abraham alone.
options.note: That title appears elsewhere in Scripture, but verse 3 specifically names Him Maker of heaven and earth.

options.text: The Rock of Israel's fathers.
options.note: This title is not used in this short psalm.

options.text: A distant, unnamed deity.
options.note: The psalm names the LORD directly and specifically, not vaguely.

quiz.q: What is Psalm 134's place among the Psalms?

options.text: It is the last of the fifteen Songs of Ascents.
options.note: It closes the pilgrim collection running from Psalm 120 to 134.

options.text: It is the opening psalm of the whole Psalter.
options.note: Psalm 1 opens the Psalter; Psalm 134 closes the Ascents collection.

options.text: It belongs to the imprecatory psalms of judgment.
options.note: The psalm is a call to blessing, not an imprecation against enemies.

options.text: It is one of the acrostic psalms.
options.note: Psalm 145, not 134, is the acrostic psalm in this section.

quiz.q: What New Testament truth most directly extends this psalm's picture of unceasing night worship?

options.text: Believers are called a holy priesthood offering a sacrifice of praise continually.
options.note: 1 Peter 2:5, 9 and Hebrews 13:15 extend exactly this calling to all believers in Christ.

options.text: Only ordained priests may worship God at all.
options.note: The New Testament extends priestly worship to all believers, not to a restricted class.

options.text: Worship should only happen once a year at a festival.
options.note: The psalm itself calls for worship beyond festival hours, into the night; the New Testament calls for unceasing praise.

options.text: Physical temples remain the only valid place of worship.
options.note: The New Testament shows Christ as greater than the temple, opening worship beyond any single building.

questions: This psalm calls the temple's unseen night watch to keep blessing the LORD. What unseen, unnoticed part of your week could become an act of worship if you saw it that way?
Verse 2 pictures worship as lifted hands toward the sanctuary. What would it look like for you to bring a physical, bodily posture of surrender into your own prayer or worship this week?
The psalm ends with a blessing flowing back from God to His worshipers. Where in your life have you experienced God's blessing following your own worship of Him, even in a hard season?
Believers are now called a holy priesthood offering praise continually. What would change in your daily rhythm if you treated even ordinary tasks as part of that continual sacrifice of praise?
The psalm closes the Songs of Ascents with worship that never stops for the night. What practice could help you carry worship into the quieter, less visible hours of your own life?

translationNotes.note: Servants who serve by night likely refers to Levites and priests keeping watch over the sanctuary through the night hours, as prescribed in passages such as 1 Chronicles 9:27.
Lift up your hands renders a gesture of prayer and praise widespread in ancient Israelite worship, an outward posture of dependence and adoration toward God.
Maker of heaven and earth is a title used elsewhere to open acts of blessing, Genesis 14:19, 22, tying the LORD's cosmic power directly to His covenant care for His worshiping people.
